items.question: Do the researchers discuss limitations, threats to validity, assumptions, or scope boundaries?
items.rationale: The paper states scope boundaries and future work, but does not provide a structured threats-to-validity or limitations section.
evidence: This paper presents the first version of the unified Modeling and Simulation (M&S) framework MOSAiC

Future work will aim to expand the simulation capabilities to include more refined orbital and environmental modeling, incorporate automated requirement tracing, automate CAD generation and time-aware thermal analyses, and explore the integration of hardware-in-the-loop or digital twin approaches.

items.question: Is the nanosatellite/CubeSat mission context and lifecycle stage described clearly enough to interpret applicability?
items.rationale: The case mission, stakeholders, small-satellite context, ConOps phases, and architecture-refinement stages are described clearly.
evidence: For validation purposes, the MOSAiC framework was applied to the design and analysis of the FIRE-EYE mission, a multi-satellite constellation dedicated to real-time wildfire detection and monitoring in the Mediterranean region.
Each state represents a distinct operational phase in the mission lifecycle, beginning with Launch, followed by Commissioning, Operational, and End-of-Life phases.

items.question: Are the MBSE method, language, toolchain, model artifacts, and system boundary described clearly enough to support replication or comparison?
items.rationale: The method, Capella/ARCADIA toolchain, PVMT extension, parser, architectural levels, simulation domains, and public repository are reported.
evidence: The system modeling process followed the ARCADIA methodology, and it was implemented using the Capella tool.
To support early validation and trade-offs, simulations were coupled with the modeling part thanks to the Property Values Management Tools (PVMT) Capella add-on [38].
All models and codes presented in this work are available in a public repository, under the GNU GPLv3 license

items.question: Are claimed outcomes explicitly linked to MBSE artifacts, MBSE activities, or model-enabled process changes rather than asserted generically?
items.rationale: Claimed outcomes are tied to Capella/ARCADIA models, PVMT properties, operational modes, parser-based extraction, and simulation feedback loops.
evidence: The architecture proposed here leverages ARCADIA-based models as authoritative sources, interfacing with simulation tools through standardized data exchanges and co-simulation strategies.

Overall, this early feedback loop enabled more informed and data-driven design decisions, provided justification for architectural refinements, and strengthened the confidence in the system's capacity to meet mission-level constraints

items.question: Is evidence provided for claimed outcomes, such as metrics, baseline comparison, case-study results, executable simulation results, model checks, stakeholder evaluation, reuse evidence, integration/test results, or flight/operational data?
items.rationale: The paper gives case-study simulations and quantitative budget outputs, but many broader claims such as reduced integration costs and improved reliability lack baselines, independent validation, or operational evidence.
evidence: Total Uplink: 57.97 MB, Total Downlink: 30.47 MB
Results show improved consistency between system models and simulation artifacts, reduced integration costs, and improved early validation of design choices.

items.question: Are requirements, verification, validation, design decisions, or lifecycle gates traced to model artifacts when such traceability is central to the paper?
items.rationale: The paper emphasizes traceability from stakeholder needs to functions, modes, architecture, and simulations, but does not present a detailed requirements trace matrix or completed automated requirements tracing.
evidence: This approach supports a clear and structured representation of the mission timeline, enabling effective traceability between operational phases and system functions.
Unlike earlier qualitative/exploratory phases, this stage features a direct linkage between formal requirement specifications and simulation results.
Future work will aim to expand the simulation capabilities to include more refined orbital and environmental modeling, incorporate automated requirement tracing

RQ1.rationale: The MOSAiC framework models small-satellite missions through ARCADIA actor/system/subsystem/component levels, operational modes, properties, and mixed-resolution simulation that can begin from coarse behavior and mature incrementally.

RQ2.rationale: The paper claims traceability, reproducibility, consistency, reduced integration costs, reliability/robustness, and integrability, but most outcomes are system-level and only partly EPS-specific, with limited comparative evidence.

RQ3.rationale: EPS is used as a detailed physical-architecture example, with PVMT properties, parser extraction, power-budget and battery simulations, and pre-implementation checks of power sufficiency and mode-dependent consumption.

bibliographic_review_management.lineage_overlap_notes: The paper cites earlier CubeSat MBSE/open-source and behavior-modeling work, including the authors' prior open-source CubeSat data formalization reference, but no prior extraction or external lineage source was consulted.

RQ1: Nanosatellite/small-satellite missions can be modeled generically using ARCADIA levels from actors to components, with operations and architecture co-defined across OA, SA, LA, and PA.

Limited behavioral knowledge is handled by beginning with coarse subsystem parameters and low-fidelity simulations, then progressively adding mode transitions, subsystem behavior, and component constraints.
Mixed-resolution extraction lets simulations use detailed PA data where available and LA abstractions elsewhere, preserving system-level analysis during partial design maturation.
RQ2: Claimed outcomes include traceability, reusability, fidelity, consistency, early validation, reduced integration costs, accessibility/reproducibility, reliability, agility, and integrability.
Reproducibility is supported by open-source tools and public models/code; reliability and cost/integration outcomes are mostly qualitative and lack baseline or operational evidence.
EPS-related outcome evidence is strongest for power-budget feasibility and early identification of energy bottlenecks, not for demonstrated flight reliability.
RQ3: Verification procedures are integrated through PVMT-enriched Capella artifacts, parser-generated simulation inputs, and simulations for design-space, performance/functional, operational-consistency, and requirement checks.

For EPS, the PA decomposes power generation, storage, regulation/control, and distribution into components and uses dynamic simulations to evaluate battery charge, eclipse behavior, and mode-dependent power demand.
The framework performs verification before physical implementation, while hardware-in-the-loop and digital-twin verification remain future work.

direct_evidence_quotes.quote: This paper presents the first version of the unified Modeling and Simulation (M&S) framework MOSAiC (Modeling and Simulation Architecture for integrated Complex systems), which connects MBSE with open source, multi-domain simulation environments
The architecture proposed here leverages ARCADIA-based models as authoritative sources, interfacing with simulation tools through standardized data exchanges and co-simulation strategies.
Simulation models are developed incrementally, starting with low-fidelity representations based on coarse overall parameters, such as general subsystem mass, volume, and power consumption.

For validation purposes, the MOSAiC framework was applied to the design and analysis of the FIRE-EYE mission, a multi-satellite constellation dedicated to real-time wildfire detection and monitoring in the Mediterranean region.
Three key simulation domains were interfaced with the MBSE model: (i) Orbital Analysis; (ii) Power Budget Simulation; (iii) Link Budget Evaluation.
Figures 12 and 13 illustrate this evolution using the Electrical Power Subsystem (EPS) as an example.
thus informing corrective actions early in the design process, before costly implementation steps were taken
All models and codes presented in this work are available in a public repository, under the GNU GPLv3 license
